en: Preface to the *Heart Sūtra* Supplement:
When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, his fundamental purpose was to illuminate the ground of the mind for sentient beings. Yet, the mind leaves no trace and is difficult to describe;
he did not stop at merely drawing a single turtle-nosed snake in empty space, with its head and tail clearly visible to behold. And yet—
It must not be touched. Now, failing to measure your own capacity, you are merely adding feet to a snake. Will you not end up being hissed at by others? Alas!
This is intended to make people know contentment and recognize the snake, like a finger pointing at the moon. Those who read this and understand it will see the snake and set aside the foot;

having grasped the meaning, they forget the snake, and only then can they be said to skillfully employ their wisdom. Furthermore, they will not disparage me. If it were otherwise, one could not avoid the venom.
If struck by this qi, one must take extreme care— take extreme care!
Written in the autumn of the Renwu year of the Chongzhen era at Dinghu Mountain by the wandering practitioner Ding.

Commentary on the Text of this Sūtra. The major sections are divided into two: first, an explanation of the title; second, the formal explanation of the sūtra text. First, the explanation of the title.

The title is divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation of the scripture’s title; second, the explanation of the translator’s name. First, regarding the explanation of the scriptural title:

the eight characters of the title *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* possess both general and specific meanings. The upper seven characters constitute the specific meaning, as they distinguish this work from all other scriptures.
Because the titles of various sūtras differ, the single character "sūtra" (jing) is general;
it applies to all sūtras because that which is spoken by the Tathāgata is uniformly called a "sūtra. Within the specific title, there are further two meanings:

the first six characters represent the dharma to be explained (*deśanīya-dharma*), while the single character "mind" (*citta*) represents the metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*) being cited. Therefore, this sūtra is established through both dharma and metaphor.

The title is "Ming" (Name). (Some say that a single dharma constitutes the name; however, the character "xin" [mind] was borrowed by the compilers to manifest the essential meaning, and is not a literal metaphor. The Mahāyāna is the teaching (*śāsana*). (This is the profound *prajñā*. Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the central tenet (*siddhānta*).
(This is the mark of the emptiness of all dharmas. Nirvāṇa is the goal (*gati*). (Ultimate nirvāṇa. The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the essence (*svabhāva*). (Form is itself emptiness.

Contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*) is the function (*karman*). (To contemplate and see the five aggregates. To explain the title comprehensively: taking divine discernment as the essence (*prajñā*), it carries one to the destination.
It serves as a function. (Pāramitā) If explained in terms of cause and effect: *prajñā* is the cause, and *pāramitā* is the fruit (reaching the other shore).
The meaning of *prajñā* is threefold: namely, the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*), and words (*vyañjana*).

Regarding *dharmatā-prajñā*, it refers to the essence of the true emptiness of the *dharmakāya*; fundamentally, it is devoid of names and characteristics. Now, within this absence of names and characteristics...

Within this, provisional names are established to discourse upon the true mark; therefore, it is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Because the source of the mind is profoundly still and tranquil, it manifests as marks despite being markless;

thus it is named the true mark. This is the true nature that is the object of contemplation; it is precisely our own fundamentally enlightened true mind, which is empty yet spiritually lucid and non-obscured.
It is neither quiescence nor illumination; its rational nature is eternally abiding, and its essence is free from arising and ceasing, as well as defilement and purity.
Regarding dharmas such as the false and illusory: the *prajñā* of contemplative illumination is the functional manifestation arising from the essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*).

It is precisely this wondrous wisdom capable of observation. This is because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profound and mysterious; were it not for this, there would be no means to discern it.

By means of this, all Buddhas wondrously accord with the *dharmakāya*, and by means of this, Bodhisattvas suddenly realize true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). This is none other than our own non-conceptual [wisdom].
Wisdom does not illuminate by means of illumination; it illuminates all dharmas such that they are all identical to true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); therefore, it is said that "form is itself emptiness. Regarding the *prajñā* of words:
words are the teachings of the Buddhas that expound principle, yet the nature of words is empty. The essence of this emptiness of nature is itself *prajñā*. Thus, the Tiantai teaching...
It is said: "Syllables are form; this form is itself the true mark (*dharmatā*). The *Tianwang Banruo Jing* (Sutra on the Prajñā of the Heavenly Kings) states:
"Dhāraṇī is without syllables, yet syllables manifest dhāraṇī. Therefore, they can clearly reveal the virtues of the two kinds of *prajñā*:
the *prajñā* of contemplation and the *prajñā* of observation. Although *prajñā* is threefold, its origin is a single mark, namely, the markless (*animitta*). That which is markless is precisely...
The Great Enlightenment is perfect and eternal; it is the essence of true emptiness. It possesses these three names, just as the world uses the character "three" [三].

If one can, for even a single thought-moment, correctly contemplate and perfectly cultivate this, illuminating and realizing that all phenomena are empty, this constitutes the perfect realization of ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
In the Sanskrit language it is *prajñā*; in the Chinese language it is "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*). "Wisdom" (*zhì*) refers to the non-conceptual wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
"insight" (*huì*) is the sublime insight within that non-conceptual wisdom, also termed "pure insight" or "formless insight. Furthermore, insight is identical to wisdom;
thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "True insight is called wisdom. This wisdom is, in its essential nature, perfectly interfused.

The freedom of illumination and function enables one to exhaustively fathom the ultimate limits of the true nature of all phenomena. This is a transcendent, wondrous, and peerless designation that surpasses ordinary sentiment and leaves behind all views;
it is not the same as the "wisdom" of worldly intellect or the "insight" of clever intelligence. Worldly wisdom and insight arise from the consciousness-mind;
they differentiate sensory objects, grasp at names and phrases, give rise to deluded knowledge and views, and serve as the basis for the outflowing roots of existence.
It is the root of birth and death; it cannot shatter the delusions of ignorance nor reveal the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Fearing that people might confuse this [term] with others, the Sanskrit sound is retained rather than being translated directly into Chinese. To investigate its reality:
there is no substance that can serve as its essence, and no dharma that can be designated by its name; yet, it is forcibly named *prajñā*. In the Sanskrit language, *pāramitā*—this...

It is translated as "reaching the other shore. If one follows the textual convention of this region, it is called "reaching the other shore," which signifies the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena without remainder.

Taking birth and death as this shore, afflictions and deluded thoughts as the currents within the ocean of suffering, and the realm of true emptiness as the other shore—since *prajñā* is like a raft for crossing over, its practice is profound.
Prajñā illuminates the emptiness of the aggregates; it extinguishes ignorance and reveals that afflictions are themselves the true mark (*dharmatā*), and that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa.
By transcending the ocean of the two deaths, one reaches the shore of the three virtues; this is called "reaching the other shore.

Those who are deluded regarding prajñā engage in various conceptual discriminations and falsely cling to body and mind as being existent. Consequently, they lose the light of wisdom and fail to understand the true mark of all phenomena.
This is called "abiding on this shore. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "I observe that all sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata;
yet, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they do not realize it. To state the essential point:

as long as even the slightest emotion remains unexhausted, one is separated from the other shore. When ordinary and sagely emotions are forgotten, one has reached the other shore—there is no other way."
It has arrived. As for "mind" (*xin*): it is like the human heart, which is the vital core of the four elements and the hundred bones.

This scripture is metaphorically the essential core to which the six hundred fascicles of the *Prajñāpāramitā* all return. If one masters this scripture, then the six hundred fascicles of the *Prajñāpāramitā* will become clear and radiant.
Some take this character to mean the "center" of the mind, asserting that this scripture occupies the central position among the six hundred fascicles.
This is an error. Some may take "mind" here to mean the "true mind" (*tathatā-citta*). However, all six hundred [scrolls] of the *Prajñāpāramitā* discourse on the true mind;

it is not unique to this sutra, for *prajñā* is itself the mind. Mind possesses both essence and function: the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the essence, and contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*) is the function.
To return the function to the essence is what is called "reaching the other shore" (*pāramitā*). Thus, the *Awakening of Faith Treatise*...
It says: "The mind itself gives rise to faith; one returns to place faith in the mind itself. The mind itself is the essence (*tī*); the arising of faith is the function (*yòng*).
To return to placing faith in the mind itself is to bring the function back to the essence. The *Huayan biexing chao* (Excerpts on the Separate Practice of the Avataṃsaka) states:

"Wisdom is the function of principle; when the essence of principle becomes wisdom, it in turn illuminates that principle. When wisdom and principle are merged in harmony, this is called true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). True wisdom is reality (*tattva*)."
The *prajñā* of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-prajñā*) is the principle of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"There is no suchness (*tathatā*) apart from wisdom that can realize it, nor is there a suchness apart from wisdom that can be entered by it. Thus, entry is the function returning to the essence.

Furthermore, since the schools of Nature (*svabhāva*) and Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)—and Emptiness (*śūnyatā*)—are each distinct, how could they be allowed to be conflated? Indeed, all six hundred [versions of the] *Prajñāpāramitā* are uniformly the emptiness of non-characteristics (*alakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Thesis: This Prajñā is the very essence of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Buddha-nature is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*);
the emptiness of the ultimate truth is called wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, it is sufficient to speak of wisdom alone; there is no need to separately speak of the "nature of mind" (*cittaprakṛti*).
If one were to speak of the nature of mind, it would become a substantial entity (*bhāva*). Once it involves a substantial entity, it is no longer empty. Or...
This refers to the mind of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Originally, it was not the title of the sutra.

Since there is no *prajñā* (wisdom) apart from the mind, and no mind apart from *prajñā*, and because the mind has no form or characteristics, it is called *prajñā*. This is the most profound and most subtle; what need is there to speak further of "mind"?
As for "sutra," it is the Sanskrit term *sūtra*, which is translated here as "Kie-ching" (Scripture of Accordance), meaning that it accords with the [truth] above.
The principle of the Buddha accords with the capacities of sentient beings at their lowest level; since people today prefer brevity, it is simply called "sūtra.
A sūtra is the teaching (*śāsana*) expounded by the Buddha, and it is defined as both "constant" (*nitya*) and "inclusive" (*saṃgraha*). "Constant" takes the meaning of being unchanging.
This means that although ancient and modern times differ, the path of awakening does not change; it cannot be thwarted by the various heterodoxies, nor can it be altered by the multitude of sages.

"Comprehensive" (*she*) refers to the thorough integration of the profound and subtle, so as to awaken those who have not yet realized it, leading them all out of the ford of suffering and onto the shore of awakening.

Therefore, if one awakens to the meaning of this sutra’s title, one reaches the other shore. (The *Bie xing chao* states: "If there is one who understands the meaning of the seven characters of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* title, then the entire [sutra]... )
The merit [of this work] has already reached its midpoint. (Pronounced *ī*). △ Second, explaining the names of the translators:
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty, by imperial decree.

"Tang" is the dynastic name. "Tripiṭaka" refers to the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras; it signifies the dharma-track and the teacher’s model, meaning that one can serve as a standard by which to instruct others through the Dharma.
"Xuanzang" is the master's dharma-name; his original name was Huì, and his secular surname was Chen.
He was a descendant of Chen Zhonggong of Taichou during the Han dynasty and the son of the scholar-recluse Huìyīng. His mother dreamed of a person in white robes...

He was born as a man in the year [blank]. At the age of eleven, he followed his elder brother, Dharma Master Changjie, to leave the household life. Daily, he was instructed in the refined principles [of the teachings].

At twenty-three, he ascended the lecture seat; his eloquence and reasoning were exquisitely thorough. Reflecting that the sutras and dharmas of this land were not yet exhaustive, he traveled to the Western Heaven (India).
There, his mastery of the Tripiṭaka was complete. He brought back to Tang China Sanskrit manuscripts of the sutras, vinaya, and śāstras, and by imperial decree, translated them.

In the language of China (Huáyán), this *Heart Sūtra* exists in a total of six translations from beginning to end. The version currently being explained is precisely that translated by the Master Xuanzang.
Regarding the term "translation" (*yì*), it means "transmission. This refers to transmitting the language of the Western Heavens (India) and rendering it into the language of Eastern Huá (China).
Part Two: The Main Explanation of the Sūtra Text, divided into two sections: First, the explicit exposition of Prajñā; Second, the implicit exposition.

The *Prajñā*. The first section, "The Exposition of Prajñā," is divided into four parts: first, revealing the Dharma through the person who practices it; second, correctly demonstrating the emptiness of phenomena;

third, cultivation and realization based upon the Dharma; and fourth, concluding praise of its efficacy. The first part, "Revealing the Dharma through the Person Who Practices It," is divided into three sections:
first, the person who is able to practice; second, the Dharma that is practiced; and third, the stages of cultivation and realization. First, the person who is able to practice.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, these five characters have both specific and general meanings. The upper three characters are specific, as they distinguish him from all other bodhisattvas;
the lower two characters are general, as this title applies to all bodhisattvas. In Sanskrit, he is called *Bhagavān Ārya-avalokiteśvara*.
In the language of China, this is translated as Guanzizai (Avalokiteśvara). If one says Āryāvalokiteśvara, it is translated as Guanshiyin (Avalokitasvara).
The Sanskrit original itself possesses these two names, as the primary intent of each respective scripture differs.

If one enters through the faculty of hearing—as in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, where the Bodhisattva enters samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation—and according to the *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra*... [text continues]

Upon hearing the mantra, Śākyamuni immediately transcended the eighth stage. All these [beings] attained the patience of non-arising through the faculty of the ear; thus they are named Avalokiteśvara.
Because he manifests function from essence, it is said that by "observing their sounds," one immediately attains liberation. The six faculties are then used interchangeably.
Therefore, he manifests a thousand hands and eyes to care for and protect all living beings. Since this sutra now enters through the faculty of the eye, it says:
"To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty, and to deliver oneself from all suffering and distress; thus one is named Avalokiteśvara.

However, this contains the meanings of both the subject and object of observation, as well as self-cultivation and the transformation of others. If the character "guan" (觀) is read with a level tone (*píngshēng*), it belongs to the observing subject (*néngguān*); "Shìyīn" (世音) [then] belongs to...
That which is observed is precisely the sentient beings to be transformed. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:

"If one single-mindedly calls upon the name of Avalokiteśvara, he immediately observes their voices, and all shall attain liberation. This refers to the subject who transforms and the objects to be transformed. The *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* says:
Because I observe and listen to the perfect clarity throughout the ten directions, the name "Avalokiteśvara" (Guanyin) pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
This combines the two faculties of eye and ear; thus it is called "observing and listening. These both pertain to one's own practice (*svayam-caryā*).

The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* includes both the titles "Avalokita" and "Īśvara," which pertain to both self and others. According to the commentary of Wēnlíng, "Avalokita" means observing the words and sounds of the world, [which are] perfect...

The title "Yuanwu" (Complete Enlightenment) likewise encompasses both self-cultivation and the transformation of others. However, from the perspective of self-cultivation, the character *guān* (contemplation) should be pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*).
This means that this Bodhisattva employs the wisdom of Prajñā-contemplation to perceive that the five aggregates—the body and mind—are empty and quiescent.

Thus, one transcends all suffering and calamity, attains liberation from birth and death, and achieves great peace and joy; therefore, it is called "sovereign freedom" (*zìzài*). This is the intersection [of the two meanings].
Guangyun: Although the character for "contemplation" (guān) is conventionally pronounced in the level tone, its actual meaning lies in the departing tone.

This is because receiving sounds is termed "hearing" (wén), while penetrating principle is termed "contemplation" (guān). Since the specific intent here is to emphasize the penetration of principle, one speaks of "contemplation" regarding sounds rather than "hearing.

Furthermore, it must be understood that what is called "one's own practice" (zìxíng) pertains to the causal stage, whereas at the stage of fruition, it constitutes "transforming others" (huàtā). However, because the Bodhisattva [acts] with benefit...
Birth is essential; yet it must necessarily be coupled with the transformation of others in order to truly correspond to the title of "Bodhisattva.
The term "Bodhisattva" is, in its full Sanskrit form, *bodhisattva*. *Bodhi* is translated here as "awakening," and *sattva* is translated as "sentient being.
Within this, there are also two meanings: self-cultivation and the transformation of others. Regarding the aspect of self-cultivation, the Bodhisattva has already possessed the wisdom of awakening.
There still remains residual habitual tendencies that have not been fully exhausted. (If these habitual tendencies were exhausted, one would be called a Buddha.
From the perspective of transforming others, it refers to the Bodhisattva who, with a heart of compassion, awakens all sentient beings and causes them to see the Great Way.
Because these two meanings are combined, the name "Bodhisattva" is used. (*Sentient beings* is a specific designation for *sattvas*). △ Second, the dharmas to be cultivated.
When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, this practice is the cultivation;
it is precisely the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) that is entered. "Profound" means extremely deep; it is precisely the *prajñā* of true emptiness.
It is not known by the mind; it cannot be cognized by consciousness. Regarding the teaching, there are two levels of *prajñā*: the deep and the shallow.

The shallow is called the *prajñā* of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-prajñā*), which is realized by those of the Two Vehicles. The deep is the *prajñā* of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-prajñā*), which is that into which Bodhisattvas enter.
This present True Emptiness and Real Mark (*tathatā*) is not something to be traversed by the limited wisdom of the partial emptiness of the Two Vehicles.
Therefore, it is called "profound. As for "time," it refers to the moment of entering and realizing the essence of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), occurring within a single *kṣaṇa*.

It is when the Bodhisattva, by means of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), illuminates the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the body and mind, such that they are vast and quiescently extinguished, and both nature and characteristics are empty.
This is precisely at the final *kṣaṇa*, the time of entering and realizing the essence of true emptiness; from this realization of the essence, [the response] arises.

It is used to cross over all suffering and calamity, and this also occurs in a single *kṣaṇa*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All take the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) as their own nature;
by means of the wondrous wisdom corresponding to a single *kṣaṇa*, one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is it.

(According to the version translated by Amoghavajra, this does not refer to the stage of the causal ground (*hetubhūmi*), but rather speaks of when a Bodhisattva enters the Samādhi of the Light of Wisdom. Now, according to this current translation, it refers to the causal ground.)

Commentary: This is intended to provide the practitioner with a point of mental focus. As the *Cittabhūmi-parivarta-sūtra* states: "A single moment of mind, when in accord with Prajñā, realizes the dharmas of the three periods of time without exception. Thus, one knows that the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*) is taken as the primary reality.

When it is said that both essence and function exist within a single moment, it is because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally empty; since suffering and affliction are thereby absent, essence and function are simultaneous. Regarding "non-conceptual wisdom" (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), it is also called fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

If, at the very first thought-moment, upon hearing a sound or seeing a form, one attains the self-nature of sound and form, this is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) occurring before one; it is the illumination of non-conceptual wisdom. It does not belong to the categories of arising and ceasing, or existence and non-existence. As soon as this wisdom arises, the discriminating mind is instantly extinguished; its very substance is true emptiness (*tathatā*).

If one perceives true emptiness, it is called seeing the Buddha-nature. If, however, one flows into the mental ground for a single *kṣaṇa* and gives rise to a second thought, discriminating between phenomena and principle, this is precisely the mind of arising and ceasing. When the delusions of arising and ceasing continue in succession, remaining unstable from moment to moment, one follows along with external sounds and forms;

thus, wisdom becomes consciousness (*vijñāna*). If one does not give rise to discrimination, the objective realm remains as it is in its suchness (*tathatā*); thus, consciousness becomes wisdom. A *kṣaṇa* is the most rapid unit of time; within a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), there are ninety *kṣaṇas*.
It is further said: "In the space of a single snap of the fingers (sixty-five *kṣaṇas*). △ Third, the stage of cultivation and realization:
"To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty, and to transcend all suffering and calamity."
"Shining illumination and seeing" refers to the contemplation that enables entry; "the five aggregates" refers to the objects of contemplation.

It is precisely by using wondrous wisdom to illuminate and see that the self-nature of the five aggregates is, in its very substance, entirely empty space. Thus, it differs from the two vehicles' practice of extinguishing form to seek emptiness.
When one realizes true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), both subject and object are forgotten. The character "illumination" (*zhào*) pertains to the fruit;

it is the "contemplation" (*guān*) in "Avalokiteśvara" (*Guānzìzài*). It pertains to the cause; it is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that does not give rise to conceptual discrimination during our ordinary, spontaneous state of mind.
Therefore, this single character "illumination" is the essential technique for the initial application of effort in the cultivation of *prajñā*. That is to say:

Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is that which, while illuminating, perceives with utter clarity. This seeing is not what is seen by the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) or the eye-consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*);

rather, it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) occurring before one. Regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), one attains the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of dharmas and does not perceive even a speck of dust that can be grasped.

This so-called "not seeing" refers to not seeing form (*rūpa*), nor seeing feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*). It is not a matter of not seeing; seeing is itself non-seeing. Because...
The five aggregates are fundamentally empty; this is precisely the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The true mark is signless (*animitta*), and therefore it cannot be seen.

To see that which cannot be seen is to penetrate the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) through and through. It is not only that one does not see the various phenomena of the mundane world, but also that one does not see any supramundane phenomena, such as all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), samādhis, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and nirvāṇa.
All are empty; therefore, nothing is seen, and this total absence of seeing is called "clearly perceiving. This is the perception of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

To have even a slight glimpse of seeing is to fall into the cave-dwelling of deluded thought and ignorance. As for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), they are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of accumulation; it refers to how all sentient beings [are constituted] by means of these five factors.
Accumulations form the body; furthermore, by means of this body, one accumulates immeasurable dust-like afflictions (*kleśa*) and undergoes the suffering of immeasurable saṃsāric cycles.
It is also called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which likewise arise from the accumulation of delusive thoughts and afflictions.
Yet these aggregates obscure the fundamental luminosity of true nature. "Form" (rūpa) takes obstruction by substance as its definition;
it refers to this body, which is a conjunctive formation of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—and thus constitutes an illusory substance.

To know that which experiences is sensation (*vedanā*); to grasp characteristics is perception (*saṃjñā*); to perform formations is volitional activity (*saṃskāra*); and to discern is consciousness (*vijñāna*). By clearly and truthfully contemplating this body and mind, one sees only the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). When seeking the marks of a person or a self, they are ultimately unobtainable; this is called "emptiness of persons" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

If one contemplates each aggregate individually, seeing that all arise from conditions and possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and that when seeking the marks of the aggregates they are unobtainable, then the five aggregates are all empty; this is called "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Thus, by illuminating the five aggregates, the principle of the two emptinesses manifests.

Regarding what is called "suffering in the world," it refers to the so-called eight sufferings: birth, aging, illness, death, encountering the hated, separation from the loved, not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates (pañca-upādāna-skandha). This means that although śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas have abandoned the mundane death of segmented existence (*bhavāgra-pratibaddha-jarāmaraṇa*), they still possess the transformation-death within lands such as those of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). For instance, an earlier stage serves as the cause and a later stage serves as the fruit; furthermore, a later stage serves as the cause and a subsequent stage serves as the fruit.

Because its causes shift and its fruits change, it is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). As for "segmented" (*bheda*), this refers to sentient beings within the three realms who, according to their karma, experience retributive fruits wherein the physical segments of their bodies vary in length and the limits of their lifespans vary in duration;

Because one perceives that the self and persons within the aggregates (*skandha*) are empty, the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are extinguished, and one transcends the suffering of segmented birth and death. Although the calamities of suffering are numerous, they are fully subsumed within these two types of death. Now, by perceiving true emptiness, one has completely transcended these calamities. II. Properly Demonstrating the Emptiness of Phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
This is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the emptiness of the aggregates; second, revealing the virtues of emptiness. First, clarifying the emptiness of the aggregates:

This correctly explains that the five aggregates are empty of self-nature. It demonstrates that emptiness is not revealed by departing from form, nor is it a void of annihilation.
Rather, the emptiness that is identical to form is true emptiness, and the form that is identical to emptiness is illusory form.
Since form is the foremost among all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the initial member is cited to encompass the subsequent ones; once the meaning of form is clarified, all phenomena become manifest.
Form is the illusory existence of the four great elements; emptiness is the principle of the true emptiness of *prajñā*.
Sentient beings, due to their delusion regarding true emptiness, give rise to the illusory existence of form. This illusory existence arises through conditions and fundamentally lacks self-nature;

Lost in the source, they chase the waves, sinking into the bitter fords of suffering. The Tathāgata teaches the wisdom of prajñā-observation to illuminate that illusory existence is no different from true emptiness;

As Master Zhigong said: "Within the body with form is the formless body; upon the road of ignorance is the path of non-arising. This is it. Emptiness.
Regarding "not different from form": True Emptiness is the substance of all phenomena; therefore, it inherently possesses all dharmas.
It is like water giving rise to waves, ripples, reflections, and foam, as well as assuming various forms such as square or round according to its vessel.

Yet, because sentient beings cling to these illusory appearances, they become deluded regarding True Emptiness—just as a fool observes the waves and becomes confused about the water. Thus, the Tathāgata teaches the cultivation of Prajñā.

Through the wisdom of contemplation, one realizes that the essence of true emptiness is no different from illusory appearances, just as one awakens to the fact that water is not different from its waves.
Therefore, it is said that "emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form. This precisely elucidates the principle of non-differentiation.

Because they are not different, they are one and the same. Furthermore, fearing that people might form attachments based on these dharmas and thus still maintain the dualistic views of form and emptiness—just as when people say jade and stone are similar, yet still regard them as two distinct things—it is said that they are "not different.

Now, wishing to dissolve these two views so that people may wondrously accord with the non-duality of form and emptiness, realizing that the whole body is this very reality, it is like waves being [identical to] water.

Water. Just as water is the wave, movement and stillness appear to be distinct, yet their substance is not of two kinds. Because one is deluded regarding true emptiness, consciousness causes the illusory to be seen as the real;

Through cultivation, one now finds that because delusion is heavy, it is necessary to illuminate with the wisdom of *prajñā*. Without the illumination of wisdom, one does not know the original reality;

They undergo birth and death. The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to emptiness and deny the existence of sin and merit; therefore, they fall into saṃsāra.

Śāriputra, all these phenomena have the characteristic of emptiness: they are neither born nor extinguished; neither defiled nor pure; neither increasing nor decreasing.
These "all phenomena" refer to the dharmas such as the five aggregates. This "characteristic of emptiness" refers to the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the ultimate emptiness of all phenomena.
Previously, it was shown that the illusory existence of the five aggregates is itself ultimate emptiness, yet their characteristic had not been explained.

Therefore, it is now shown: "This is the mark of the emptiness of all dharmas. Since it is said to be the mark of the emptiness of all dharmas, one cannot speak of the mark of emptiness separately from all dharmas.
This directly points to the very substance of all dharmas as being the mark of true emptiness.
It is like the moon in water or a reflection in a mirror; its substance is free from arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase and decrease. Therefore, it cannot be conceptualized.
One attempts to cause it to arise, to destroy it so that it ceases, to defile it with impurity, to purify it through cultivation, to augment it, or to diminish it.

Why is this? Because those reflections lack substantial reality; their very substance is emptiness, just like space, and cannot be designated by such terms as arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase and decrease. The characteristic of true emptiness is likewise so.

Therefore, it cannot be named; it is only forcibly designated as "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The characteristic of true reality cannot be glimpsed by the five eyes nor measured by the intellect or mind;

Deluded regarding the truth and pursuing the false, one perceives arising and ceasing. Within the twelve links of dependent origination, there are two gates: that of transmigration and that of cessation.
The gate of transmigration consists of the two truths of suffering and its origin; as these are the causes and effects of the mundane world, they are defiled.

The gate of cessation consists of the two truths of the path and its extinction; as these are the causes and effects of the supramundane, they are pure. In the cultivation of the Bodhisattva, the path...

What is now spoken of as the non-arising and non-extinction, and the absence of defilement, purity, increase, and decrease, is intended to reveal that within the true mark of emptiness of all phenomena, there are fundamentally no dharmas such as ordinary beings and sages, or the causes and fruits of cultivation and realization;
it directly manifests the single body of the true emptiness of *prajñā*, causing people to shed all views so that not even a single thread remains clinging to them.

Truly manifesting the eternal and constant is precisely the Tathāgata (as stated in the *Huan-yuan guan*: "Following the current with added defilement does not stain it; reversing the flow to remove defilement does not purify it. Abiding in the body of a sage it does not increase;

Moreover, when obstructions are exhausted there is no decrease; when virtues are fulfilled there is no increase. This is divided into four parts: first, an explanation of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu); second, an explanation of the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda); third, an explanation of the four noble truths (catvāri āryasatyāni);
and fourth, an explanation of wisdom and attainment. First, the explanation of the aggregates, bases, and elements.
Therefore, in emptiness there is no form; no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
There is no form, sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or phenomenon. There is no realm of the eye, and so forth, up to no realm of mental consciousness.

"Is hence" (*iti*) is a term used to connect what precedes with what follows, serving to elucidate the reason why all phenomena possess the characteristic of emptiness—such as being neither arising nor ceasing—and thus lack form, sensation, and so forth.
