because the true reality of ultimate emptiness is fundamentally detached from all dharmas, whether mundane or supramundane, there are no aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), or cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Regarding the characteristics of realization: when one reaches the emptiness of *prajñā*, even the nature of emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*);
therefore, it is said to be "non-existent. This non-existence is not the same as the non-existence of a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns;

rather, it is the very state wherein all characteristics are present yet all characteristics are transcended, constituting non-existence. When deluded sentiments cease, the dualistic views of ordinary beings and sages are dissolved, and the True [Nature]...

Emptiness is revealed in its nakedness; therefore, no aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), or elements (*dhātu*) can be apprehended. The absence of form through to formations and consciousness constitutes the absence of the five aggregates.
The absence of the eye through to contact and mental objects (*dharma*) constitutes the absence of the twelve bases.

The absence of the eye-element through to the absence of the mind-consciousness-element constitutes the absence of the eighteen elements. These [elements] combine the six faculties and the six objects to form the twelve bases.

(The sense faculties [indriya] have the meaning of being able to produce consciousness; the objects [viṣaya] have the meaning of defiling the emotional consciousness. Combining the six sense faculties, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses constitutes the eighteen elements (dhātus).
Internally there are the six sense organs (*indriya*); externally there are the six objects (*viṣaya*). When the organ and the object encounter one another, consciousness arises between them.

These are what are called eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. (The term *dhātu* [realm/element] has the meaning of "distinct differentiation.

This means that these eighteen factors each have their own distinct essence, so that their meanings do not become confused or intermingled. For example, the eye takes form as its realm; the ear takes sound as its realm; and so on, up to the mind taking mental phenomena (*dharma*) as its realm. The eye cannot transcend form in its seeing, and the ear cannot transcend sound in its hearing.)... and so forth.

The ultimate intention cannot transcend the fact that there is cognition. Form has the eye as its sphere, because form is necessarily what is seen by the eye; it is not sound, fragrance, or other such objects that can confront the eye. This continues up to the mind, which has mental phenomena (*dharma*) as its sphere, because mental phenomena are necessarily what is known by the mind.

Because sounds, odors, and so forth cannot serve as objects for the mind, the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) is the consciousness belonging to the eye; it necessarily arises depending upon the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) and cannot arise depending on any other faculty. Furthermore, the eye itself cannot produce the consciousnesses of sound, odor, and so forth. Therefore, this [element] is distinct [from the others]. The others can be understood by analogy.

The term "up to" (*yāvat*) indicates the beginning and end, thereby encompassing what lies between them. These aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are called the three categories of the Dharma-gates (*dharmamukha*).
Although there are three Dharma-gates, they generally comprise the two types of phenomena: matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*); thus, they are established through various combinations and expansions.
They are different. For those who are deluded regarding the mind but not regarding form, the Buddha taught the Dharma of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);

he combined form into one part and opened the mind into four parts (since sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all parts of the mind). For those who are deluded regarding form but not regarding the mind, he taught the Dharma of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*);
he opened form into ten and a half parts (namely, the five internal sense organs and the six external objects, with the dharma-object accounting for half a part) and combined the mind into one part.

Half [of the mental object]—that is, one part of the faculty of mind (manas-indriya) and half of the mental object (dharma-viṣaya)—is taught as the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśa-dhātu) for those who are deluded regarding both mind and form.

[This is to be understood accordingly: form is divided into ten and a half parts, and the mind is opened into seven and a half parts—namely, the six consciousnesses of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, plus one part of the faculty of mind and half of the mental object.
Thus, the Tathāgata, in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, teaches these three categories of dharmas, each according to their respective faculties and natures.
By practicing a single dharma, one is able to realize and enter [the truth]. Now, within this gate of the *prajñā* of true emptiness, none of these things exist at all;
therefore, it is said that they are "non-existent. This precisely reveals that the essence of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of true emptiness is not a substance of obstruction.

Because it lacks the characteristics of sensation, reception, perception, mental formations, and discernment—namely, the marks of feeling, apperception, volitional activity, and accumulation—it is devoid of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This is the true mark of true emptiness.
The substance is neither sense organ nor object; it is the characteristic of that which enters and that which is entered. Therefore, there are no twelve bases (*āyatana*).

True emptiness and the true mark have a substance that is not the characteristic of the discrimination between sense organs and objects. Therefore, there are no eighteen realms (*dhātu*). △ Second, the explanation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; and so on, up to no aging and death, nor is there the exhaustion of aging and death.

This is called the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), and it is also called "dependent arising" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) or "dependent production. That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition...

Feeling (*vedanā*). Feeling conditions craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Craving conditions grasping (*upādāna*). Grasping conditions becoming (*bhava*). Becoming conditions birth (*jāti*). Birth conditions old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

As for "ignorance" (*avidyā*), it means the sense of darkness and obscurity. (This refers to the delusions of afflictions from past lives which shroud the true nature; lacking the clarity of wondrous awakening, one falsely identifies the four elements as the characteristics of the self-body and the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects as the characteristics of one's own mind.

Therefore, it is called ignorance. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "It exists in such a way that it is non-existent. If one cannot thoroughly comprehend such dharmas that are non-existent, this is termed ignorance.")

What phenomena are non-existent? They are the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), one discriminates and clings to the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism;

because of this, one neither knows nor sees the nature of the non-existence of all phenomena. *Saṃskāra* (formations): This refers to the performance [of action]. That is to say, it is the past performance of wholesome and unwholesome karma by means of body and speech;

therefore, they are called formations. *Vijñāna* (consciousness): This is the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*). [The union of] the true and the false is termed consciousness. Because of the mutual attraction of past afflictions and karma, this spiritual consciousness is caused to enter and take rebirth in a mother’s womb. *Nāman* (name).

"Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): "name" refers to the mind, and "form" refers to the body. (From the time of entering the mother's womb until the fifth week, the various sense organs and physical forms arise, along with the differentiation of the four limbs;

this is called name-and-form. "The six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*) refers to the six faculties. (From after name-and-form until the seventh week, the six faculties unfold and possess the function of entering the six objects; therefore, they are called the six sense bases.)

"Contact" (*sparśa*) is also called the "six sense bases. It means "impingement. (From the time of birth until the age of three or four, although the six sense organs impinge upon the six objects, one is not yet able to discern them and give rise to perceptions of pleasure or pain;

therefore, it is called contact. "Feeling" (*vedanā*) is "reception. (From the age of five or six until the age of twelve or thirteen, because of the external six objects impinging upon the six sense organs, one is able to receive the qualities of the preceding objects, such as their being pleasant or unpleasant;

however, one is still unable to give rise to thoughts of sexual desire and so forth; therefore, it is called feeling. "Craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) is "thirsty attachment. (From the age of fourteen or fifteen until eighteen...)

At nine years of age, one craves the objects of sensory desire, such as noble lineage and exquisite things; however, because one has not yet extensively and universally pursued them, this is called *tṛṣṇā* (craving). *Upādāna* (clinging) means seeking and grasping.

(From the age of twenty onwards, craving and desire increase further, and one extensively and universally rushes about in pursuit of the five sensory objects; therefore, it is called clinging. *Bhava* (existence) refers to future existence.

(Because of rushing about in pursuit of various objects, one gives rise to wholesome and unwholesome karma, which accumulates and draws forth the tainted fruits of rebirth within the three realms; therefore, it is called existence. *Jāti* (birth) refers to taking birth. (The wholesome and unwholesome karma performed in this present life...)

The world returns to take birth within the six realms and four modes of existence; therefore, it is called "birth. "Old age and death" refers to decay and disintegration (meaning that after taking birth in a future life, the body composed of the five aggregates decays and subsequently disintegrates;
this is called old age and death). These twelve factors induce results through their mutual succession, and are thus called "causes"; they depend upon one another.
This is called "conditioning. It continues and revolves through the three periods of time without interruption, like the turning of a wheel; therefore, it is called "saṃsāra" (wheeling).
It begins with ignorance and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) in the past life acting as causes, which evoke the five results in the present life:
consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling. From these present results, there arise craving, grasping, and becoming (*bhava*).
The present cause: by means of the present cause, one brings about the fruit of birth, aging, and death in future lives;
this is the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), which is the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and is called the gate of cyclic existence (*pravṛtti-mukha*).

If a *pratyekabuddha* realizes that these phenomena arise through conditions—such that with the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā-nirodha*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) cease, and so on up to the cessation of aging and death—this is the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), which is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

The awakening to dharmas is called the gate of cessation. If one uses the wisdom of *prajñā* to illuminate and realize that the essential nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) is entirely empty and devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing, it is said:
"There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance," and so on, up to "there is no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death.
To say "there is no ignorance" is to point out that the initial characteristic of the process of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) is empty; likewise, [there is no]...
"The exhaustion of ignorance" indicates the emptiness of the initial phase of cessation. Up to "no old age and death" indicates the emptiness of the final phase of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, "no exhaustion of old age and death" indicates the emptiness of the final phase of cessation. "Exhaustion" is synonymous with "cessation."

This is likely to cite the beginning and end as empty, thereby encompassing the middle, in order to reveal that the essence of the *prajñā* of true emptiness is not characterized by the phases of transmigration or cessation;
therefore, it is devoid of the twelve links of dependent origination. △ Third, the explanation of the Four Noble Truths.
There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path.
Suffering refers to the fruit of suffering, which is birth and death (*saṃsāra*). The origin refers to the causes of suffering, which are afflictions and karma;

these constitute the cause and effect of the mundane world. Cessation refers to the fruit of bliss, which is *nirvāṇa*. The path refers to the causes of bliss, which are the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); these constitute the cause and effect of the supramundane. Wisdom...
The *Dulun* (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā) states: "The world and the body are the fruit of suffering; craving, hatred, ignorance, and all other afflictions (*kleśa*) are the causes of suffering;
the cessation of afflictions is the cessation of suffering; and the method for extinguishing afflictions is called the Path.
The Tathāgata taught these Four Noble Truths primarily for the sake of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, who do not understand the three realms and the five aggregates.
The Dharma is like an illusion and like a magical transformation; it is fundamentally unborn from the beginning, its nature and characteristics being quiescent and extinguished.
Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream from yesterday. Yet within this unborn Dharma, one falsely perceives arising and ceasing, and thus undergoes the cycle of saṃsāra in vain.
It is like a mirage in a place where there is no water, where one falsely conceives the notion of water and merely exhausts oneself in toil. Therefore, the Tathāgata causes them to know this.

To sever suffering and eliminate its origin, to aspire toward cessation and cultivate the path—this merely provides a temporary respite from the root of suffering. The Śrāvakas do not fully comprehend this;
they become attached to the bliss of nirvāṇa and take it to be a true realization. Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas, however, practice the contemplation of *prajñā* and perceive the principle of true emptiness.

They see that there is no dharma of cultivation or realization involving arising and ceasing, because the self-nature of arising, ceasing, cultivation, and realization is empty. Therefore, it is said that there is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path.

(“Truth” (*satya*) means that which is examined and verified. Although ordinary beings experience suffering and its origin, they do not examine them as reality; thus, these cannot be called truths. Because the non-erroneous noble wisdom examines and knows the objects, they are called the Noble Truths (*ārya-satya*). As for the “factors of enlightenment,” these are the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*);
details may be found in other sūtras and śāstras). △ Fourth, the explanation of the attainment of wisdom.
"There is neither ignorance nor attainment.
Here, "wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to the wisdom that is capable of contemplation; "attainment" (*prāpti*) refers to the principle that is realized.

The intent is to clarify that there is not only an absence of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), truths (*satya*), and conditions (*pratyaya*), but also an absence of the persons of the three vehicles who realize [the truth] as well as the objects realized, and even the Bodhisattva who cultivates *prajñā*.
The wisdom that perceives all phenomena as empty, and even the principle attained through that wisdom of emptiness, do not exist. This is because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like space.
Due to the affliction of cataracts, one perceives flowers in the sky and grasps them as real; therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Those who wish to know the secret meaning and intent of the teachings on how the Tathāgata cannot realize any Buddha-dharmas should study this profound [wisdom]."
The Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this? Because the Buddha-dharmas to be realized and the one who realizes them are unobtainable.

Furthermore, it says: within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of all phenomena, the one who realizes, that which is realized, the place of realization, the time of realization, and that by means of which one realizes—whether combined or separate—all these are unobtainable and invisible. Thus, the Bodhisattva...
Regarding the emptiness of all phenomena, one should not realize it. That is to say, when contemplating the emptiness of phenomena, one first forms this thought:

"I should contemplate that all characteristics of phenomena are empty, yet I should not realize this. I contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena for the sake of training, not for the sake of realization.
This continues until: "At this time, regarding my unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment..."

One should train [in this], but one should not realize it as a goal. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because Bodhi deeply penetrates emptiness, one knows that emptiness is also empty and Nirvāṇa is also empty;
therefore, there is nothing to be realized. This is because neither the dharma of realization nor the dharma of non-realization can be apprehended."
Beginning from the five aggregates and ending with the four noble truths, these constitute the objects of contemplation for those practicing the path of the three vehicles.
Now, when one cultivates Prajñā, it is like a great mass of fire: regardless of whether it is pure or impure, everything touched by it is consumed.

Therefore, the principle of true emptiness is revealed, and all ordinary sentiments are swept away. Within this state of True Suchness, the realm of the sages, even the "wisdom of all wisdoms" (sarvajñajñāna) cannot be apprehended. Thus...
The aggregates, bases, and elements of the world, the four truths and dependent origination that transcend the world, and even the realization and that which is realized—all are empty.
Thus, both person and phenomena are forgotten, and object and wisdom are simultaneously extinguished. It is like when the illness is gone, the medicine is discarded;
hence it is said: "There is no wisdom and there is no attainment. △ Third, the section on practicing and realizing according to the Dharma. Part two: First, clarifying what the Bodhisattva attains.
Nirvāṇa, Part Two: Clarifying that all Buddhas attain Bodhi. First, clarifying that Bodhisattvas attain Nirvāṇa because there is nothing to be attained.
Because the Bodhisattva relies on the Prajñāpāramitā, his mind is without hindrance.
Because he is without hindrance, he is free from fear. Far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, he reaches ultimate Nirvāṇa.
The phrase "because there is nothing to be attained" refers back to the various instances of the word "non-" mentioned above.
It means that because all dharmas are non-attainable as previously stated, the Bodhisattva relies upon this and cultivates it until attaining ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, this word "non-" unifies the essential purport of the entire sutra; for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is suchness (*tathatā*), its essence being fundamentally quiescent and extinguished. If, by means of...
To have a mind that grasps at attainment is to be deluded regarding the original reality and to lose the wisdom of prajñā-observation.
By what means could one thereby distance oneself from inversion and attain ultimate nirvāṇa? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which has nothing to be attained is called wisdom."
Because Bodhisattvas have attained this wisdom, it is called "non-attainment. Furthermore, that which is non-attainment is called Great Nirvāṇa.
Because Bodhisattvas abide securely within Great Nirvāṇa and do not perceive the intrinsic nature or characteristics of any phenomena, it is called non-attainment.
Moreover, that which is non-attainment is called the Mahāyāna. Because Bodhisattvas do not dwell in any phenomena, it is so named.
Regarding the Mahāyāna, Qingliang (Jizang) said: "Non-attainment is the characteristic of *prajñā*. It is only by attaining the wisdom of non-attainment through *prajñā* that one truly attains it.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "One takes non-attainment as the skillful means (*upāya*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are two kinds of emptiness: first, emptiness without skillful means, which causes one to fall to the level of the Two Vehicles; second, emptiness with skillful means."

Emptiness means there is nowhere to fall, leading directly to unsurpassed bodhi. Furthermore, there are two kinds of emptiness: first, the emptiness of mere practice, which leads to falling into the stages of the two vehicles;
second, the emptiness of the unattainability of practice, wherein even emptiness itself is unattainable, and thus there is no place to fall.
Therefore, all bodhisattvas, through the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya*) and the insight of *prajñā*, illuminate the emptiness of all phenomena. Thus, regarding...
The aggregates, bases, elements, causes, conditions, and truths, as well as the means of realization and that which is realized, are all unapprehendable.
By means of this mind of non-apprehension, one practices in reliance upon prajñā; thus, the burden of karma is liberated.
Because one practices in reliance upon this, afflictions do not obstruct the mind and objects do not obstruct wisdom; therefore, the mind is without hindrance. Due to this lack of hindrance...
When obstructions are removed, the accumulation of karma is liberated. Because karma is liberated, one is externally free from the terrors of the retributive fruits of the three realms.
Due to the absence of such fruits, one is internally and eternally freed from the delusions and inverted dreams of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Through this freedom from afflictions, true permanence is revealed alone; this is ultimate *nirvāṇa*. This reveals the essence of the *prajñā* of true emptiness.

It is neither arising nor ceasing; it is to violate the cause and lose the fruit. Therefore, all Bodhisattvas find nothing to be apprehended in any phenomenon, and this is the attainment of ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
Indeed, the entire great *Prajñāpāramitā* takes "non-apprehension" as its fundamental principle.
Even if there were a single phenomenon that transcended *nirvāṇa*, it would likewise be like a dream or an illusion—entirely unapprehendable.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: Although they realize that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, bodhisattvas nevertheless, by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and deliver immeasurable multitudes.
Although they realize enlightenment, there is nothing realized; even the realization of the dharma of non-realization is entirely non-existent.
Because it can be attained, yet through its unattainability, there is no subject that realizes nor any object realized, and all deluded cognitions and views vanish.
Since there are no deluded views, there are no afflictions of inversion. If there were anything realized, that would itself be a deluded dream and fantasy.
How could one attain nirvāṇa and bodhi? The *Vajraprajñā-anabhinna-prajñapti-śāstra* states:
"When discussing the time when a bodhisattva realizes reality, even the dharmakāya is not attained.
A bodhisattva is the person who relies [upon the teaching], while prajñāpāramitā is the dharma upon which they rely; the mind is free from obstruction.
Obstructions, inversions, and delusive dreams are the hindrances to this capacity for emptiness. Ultimate nirvana is the fruit to be realized. As for ultimate nirvana:

when the five stages of dwelling are completely exhausted and the two types of death have forever ceased, it is called "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*) and also called "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*), because it is the limit where nirvana is fully consummated.
It is further termed "nirvana without abode" (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*), which is not the same as—

The two vehicles merely distance themselves from the afflictions of views and thought; this is termed "liberation. They have provisionally attained the *nirvāṇa* of the illusory city, which is truly not ultimate.

In Sanskrit it is called *nirvāṇa*; in Chinese it is called "perfect quiescence" (*yuánjì*). "Perfect" (*yuán*) means that there are no virtues that are not complete. "Quiescent" (*jì*) means that there are no obstructions that are not exhausted.

It is also translated as "Great Parinirvāṇa" (*dà mièdù*). "Great" (*dà*) refers to the true mark (*shíxiàng*). "Extinguished" (*miè*) refers to the emptiness of the aggregates (*yùn*). "Crossed over" (*dù*) refers to...
Transcending suffering, moreover, "Great" is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), "Extinction" is liberation (*vimukti*), and "Crossing over" is wisdom (*prajñā*).

When a Bodhisattva cultivates wisdom and contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena, the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) becomes manifest. One realizes that the illusory body of birth and death is none other than the original Dharma-body;
that afflictions are themselves wisdom; and that the karma of fetters is itself liberation. Thus, the three obstacles are suddenly emptied and the three virtues are perfected.

This is called ultimate *nirvāṇa*. (As for the three obstacles: they are the obstacle of karma, the obstacle of retribution, and the obstacle of afflictions. Karma can bind sentient beings within the prison of birth and death so that they cannot attain liberation;

therefore, it is called "impediment. The retributive fruits of the triple world are like a burning house and possess a terrifying aspect; therefore, they are called "fear. The essential nature of ignorance is a perverted dharma, like a dream;

therefore, it is called "perverted dreams and thoughts. By being free from afflictions, one does not give rise to delusions, fetters, or karmic actions. By being free from these fetters and karmic actions, there is no retribution. (The five abodes refer to the delusions of the five stages of abiding. These delusions cause sentient beings to dwell and cling to birth and death. First: all views.

1. Dwelling in views (*dṛṣṭi-vāsa*): this refers to the afflictions of view within the three realms. 2. Dwelling in desire for sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga-vāsa*): this refers to the afflictions of thought within the desire realm. 3. Dwelling in desire for form (*rūparāga-vāsa*): this refers to the afflictions of thought within the form realm.

4. Dwelling in desire for existence (*bhavarāga-vāsa*): this refers to the afflictions of thought within the formless realm. 5. Dwelling in ignorance (*avidyā-vāsa*): this refers to the fundamental ignorance-affliction. Because the followers of the Two Vehicles have not yet fully understood these afflictions, they remain stagnant in emptiness and dwell in the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*). Mahayana Bodhisattvas, having severed them through expedient means, yet still have residual afflictions that are not yet exhausted;

therefore, they dwell in the Land of True Reward (*sambhoga-bhūmi*). Now, by practicing Prajñā, these residual afflictions are suddenly shattered; hence it is called "ultimate. II. Explaining how all Buddhas attain Bodhi.
The Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present—rely upon the *prajñāpāramitā* and thereby attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"The three periods" refers to the past, the future, and the present. "*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" [is the supreme, perfect enlightenment].
This term, in the language of China, means "Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment" (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). It refers to the path realized by all Buddhas.

The intent is to clarify that not only do Bodhisattvas attain *nirvāṇa* by relying on *prajñā* with a mind of non-attainment, but all Buddhas of the three periods of time likewise attain unsurpassed *bodhi* by relying on *prajñā* with a mind of non-attainment. Thus, both *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* [are attained in this manner].
Originally there are no two paths; all are attained by relying upon Prajñā. Apart from this Prajñā, there is no one who attains it.
Thus, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra says: "All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, ride upon such a vehicle."
Practicing this path, one arrives at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
One should know that this vehicle and this path are none other than the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The emptiness of the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena is itself *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It further states: "The Bodhisattva practices *prajñā*..."
Having become a Buddha, [the state] is renamed *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Bodhi is the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*);

nirvāṇa is the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). Although bodhi and nirvāṇa are two distinct names, both are the fruits of the two-fold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) realized by the Ultimate Sage.
For if afflictions were not eliminated through wisdom, they would not be severed; and if wisdom were not the result of such severance, it would not be perfected.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Because the Bodhisattva has already perfected the path to enlightenment and all the *pāramitās*, by means of the sublime wisdom associated with a single moment, they realize the Tathāgata’s omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
At that time, because the continuity of all afflictions and habitual tendencies never arises again, it is called 'abandonment without remainder.'"
Thus, one is named a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. It should be known that these two fruits are both accomplished by relying upon the Prajñāpāramitā.

As for "Buddha," in the Sanskrit language it is fully called *Buddha*; in the Chinese language it is translated as "Awakening" (*Jue*), a term signifying the exhaustive realization of principle and the full perfection of nature.
This refers to what is called awakening to the true permanence of nature and understanding the falsity of delusion. To exercise [this] without...
Based on loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he delivers the realm of sentient beings; because his practice is fulfilled and his fruit is perfected, he is called the Great Awakened One (*Mahābuddha*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Because he has naturally awakened to all phenomena, he is named Buddha (*Buddha*);
because he awakens all sentient beings to reality as it is, causing them to leave behind inverted views, evil karma, and manifold sufferings, he is named Buddha. For what reason?
It is called *bodhi*. The realization of the meaning of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the realization of the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness) constitute the meaning of *bodhi*.

Because it is the true, pure, and wondrous awakening of all Buddhas, it is named *bodhi*. Because all Buddhas, by means of this, manifestively awaken to all aspects of all phenomena (*sarvākāra-sarvadharma*), it is named *bodhi*.

As for the *Tathāgata*, it is so called because he has come (*āgata*) by way of the path of former Buddhas to achieve perfect awakening; thus he is the "Thus-Come One. Furthermore, he illuminates the characteristics of all phenomena, whether there be Buddhas or not.

The Buddha is such because he has realized, as it truly is, the nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which is the natural order of phenomena. Thus, he is called the Tathāgata. Furthermore, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata has realized, as it truly is, the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas—its non-falsity and its immutability.

Because he has awakened to this characteristic of suchness, he is designated as the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Regarding "wisdom-virtue" (jñānaguṇa): it refers to the illumination and clear comprehension of all dharmas through impartial wisdom, attaining unimpeded penetration and responding to the capacities of sentient beings.

He expounds it for them without error. As for the fruit of the cessation of defilements (*prahāṇa-guṇa*): it means that all afflictions, delusions, and karmic actions have been severed and purified until nothing remains. Wherever he dwells among those to be transformed, evil cannot stain him; he acts with sovereign ease, free from all burdens and fetters.

Regarding the second, the fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parivṛtti-phala*): because he realizes that afflictions are themselves bodhi, he transforms afflictions and relies upon bodhi—this is the path realized by all Buddhas.

Because he realizes that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself nirvāṇa, he transforms birth-and-death and relies upon nirvāṇa—this is the fruit realized by all Buddhas. △ Fourth, the conclusion praising its efficacy.
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, an unequaled mantra;
it is able to eliminate all suffering, for it is true and not false.
Therefore, it should be known that both Bodhisattvas and Buddhas all rely upon this profound Prajñā to realize nirvāṇa and bodhi.
For this reason, one knows that the efficacy of Prajñā is inconceivable;

it cannot be fully expressed through names, words, numbers, or quantities, but is instead praised and illustrated by means of four kinds of mantras. "Spirit" (shen) takes the meaning of being unfathomable as its definition. It clarifies—
It is able to destroy darkness; that is to say, the divine power and wondrous function of this *prajñā* cannot be known by the measure of the mind.

It can extinguish the dark ignorance of delusion and manifest the principle of true emptiness and wisdom (*śūnyatā-jñāna*). By realizing *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, there is no further dharma that transcends it;
therefore, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). As it is the secret heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of all Buddhas, it is likewise without [superior].
There is no dharma that can be compared to it; therefore, it is called "unequaled" (*asama-sama*).
Furthermore, this Prajñā is named the "Incomparable Dharma," and there is likewise no incomparable dharma with which it can be compared; thus, it is called "unequaled.

The fetters of the five abodes are exhausted, the two types of death have both perished, the fruits of the four modes of birth have ceased, and all myriad burdens are entirely eliminated; therefore, it is said that it "can remove all suffering. As...
The wondrous function of this *prajñā* is inconceivable: it realizes the false as the true and transforms the ordinary into the holy.
It will certainly bring an end to suffering without doubt; thus, it is specifically intended for sentient beings to believe, accept, and practice, and is therefore said to be "truly not false.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "When studying this great king of mantras, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, although [one may have doubts] regarding me and the Dharma..."

There is nothing to be attained, yet one is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. (The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: For what reason is Prajñā called the Great Bright Mantra?)

It refers to those non-Buddhists who possess various incantations and arts that benefit the people and can fulfill their every desire; they command ghosts and spirits, attain great renown, and cause the people to submit to them.

Among all such incantations, the Prajñāpāramitā is the supreme incantation, for it constantly bestows upon sentient beings the joy of the Way and its virtue (*mārga-guṇa*). Other incantations can give rise to the afflictions of greed and hatred, allowing one to act with self-indulgence and fall into the three evil realms.

This *prajñāpāramitā* incantation, however, can extinguish all attachments to meditative concentration, the Buddha-way, and *nirvāṇa*, let alone the coarse diseases of greed and hatred. For this reason, it is called the Great Bright Incantation, the Unsurpassed Incantation, and the Peerless Incantation. Furthermore, this incantation can cause people to leave behind old age, sickness, death, and suffering, and it can establish them [in liberation].

Regarding the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), it enables practitioners to become the greatest among all sentient beings; therefore, it is called a "Great Mantra. Because it can provide such benefit, it is named "Unsurpassed. In ancient times, there were rishis who possessed mantras capable of knowing the minds of others, known as *yakṣaṇī*; mantras capable of flying and transforming, known as *gandharvī*;

and mantras capable of extending one's lifespan beyond a thousand or ten thousand years. Among all such mantras, none could equal them. Within these peerless mantra-arts—*yakṣaṇī*, *gandharvī*, and the longevity-mantras—[this Great Vehicle surpasses them].

The Prajñāpāramitā transcends and surpasses the immeasurable; therefore, it is called "the Peerless" (asama-sama). Furthermore, the dharmas of all Buddhas are called "equal" (sama), yet because the Prajñāpāramitā is the causal condition for attaining Buddhahood, it is called "the Peerless.

Moreover, among all sentient beings, the Buddhas are called "unequaled" (asama); this Prajñā-mantra was produced by the Buddhas, and is therefore called the "Peerless Mantra. 2. The Secret Teaching of Prajñā.
Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* mantra is spoken. It is spoken as follows: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
This secret exposition of *prajñā* is the inconceivable realm; its essence is true emptiness, which is no different from the explicit teaching. However—
This is explained for the sake of clarity. I fear that people might rely on the literal text to interpret the meaning, or rely on the exposition to give rise to views;
they might further cling to the notion that "true emptiness" possesses a substantial essence, thereby turning it into a real dharma that becomes subject to arising and ceasing.

Failing to realize that true emptiness is itself empty, they instead give rise to attachment and fall back into ignorance. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty; emptiness..."
By nature, one should not cling to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended; how much less can there be an empty nature that can cling to emptiness?
Thus, failing to realize that true emptiness is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*), one seeks wisdom with wisdom.

Wisdom then becomes conceptual understanding (*vijñapti*); understanding, in turn, distorts the truth. This gives rise to a mind of illumination; illumination establishes objects. Following illumination, one loses the essence. To turn back—
This constitutes the matter of forming shadows. Thus, great wisdom, though residing right before one's eyes, is inverted into the realm of names and forms.
Therefore, Yongjia said: "Without leaving this very place, it is ever serene; seek it, and you will know it cannot be seen.

Now, this esoteric teaching of Prajñā is precisely intended to cause the human mind to forget its intellect and for wisdom to vanish, so that without relying on seeking, true emptiness manifests before one. Suddenly...
Yet, silent realization exceeds even the tally and seal; therefore, it is called a *dhāraṇī*.
It is the inconceivable, secret, and true speech of the Tathāgata, which prays that sentient beings may be no different from the Buddha.

For this reason, the practitioner who recites it should empty the mind and unify the thought, maintaining an uninterrupted succession of moments—just as the *guoluo* (wasp) chants its spell over the *mingling* (caterpillar), and [the transformation] occurs naturally.

The profound delusion accords with the Truth; thus, one becomes a sage from being an ordinary person. Some say that the exoteric teaching is intended to bring understanding and generate wisdom, thereby extinguishing the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
the esoteric teaching is intended to prompt recitation and generate merit, thereby extinguishing the obstacle of karmic offenses (*karmāvaraṇa*).

Others offer a forced interpretation, translating *gate* as "crossing over," *pāra* as "the other shore," and *saṃgha* as "the assembly," asserting that it means "crossing over for oneself and crossing over for others, arriving together with the assembly."
To explain "bodhi" as "the other shore" (*pāra*) in such a manner is to deviate from the ultimate principle and entirely miss the intention of the Sage.

Since it is said to be taught cryptically, how could anyone understand it? It is beyond the comprehension even of Bodhisattvas at the stage of causes who are not yet saints; how much less could ordinary, ignorant people fathom it?
This can be explained through principle: names and words are both transcended, and phenomena and principle are both forgotten. Even with the *śakara* eye, one cannot grasp it by looking or feeling;
once it falls into the realm of thought, it immediately becomes the dregs of knowledge and views. To establish knowledge within knowledge is the very root of ignorance.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is thereby established; for ten thousand kalpas one remains submerged and lost. By what means can all suffering and calamity be transcended?
When mental activity ceases and cognitive perception is extinguished, ignorance is shattered and the other shore (*pāra*) is reached.
